title: Shared Responsibility Is the New Leadership
author: Kathleen Schafer
summary: Schafer argues that the myth of the heroic leader who carries responsibility for everyone is collapsing because concentrated control is brittle under complexity. In its place she proposes shared responsibility: cultures in which responsibility is distributed, trusted and coordinated, and people participate rather than being managed into compliance. She warns against the pendulum reflex of lurching to the opposite of what failed and urges investment in slow, relational systems-change work before crisis forces a response. She ends by asking readers to stop waiting to be appointed and to lead with one another.
points: Concentrating responsibility at the top is brittle under stress, so the heroic-leader model fails when complexity rises.
Shared responsibility is a cultural shift, not a management tactic: distributed, trusted and coordinated rather than chaotic.
Reacting in opposition to what failed tends to recreate the old problems, so healthier systems must be imagined and practiced in advance.
Systems change needs sustained, relational support, not only emergency relief.
Leaders should move from critique to participation rather than wait for an invitation.
quotes: Not because leadership no longer matters, but because concentrating responsibility at the top has proven brittle in the face of complexity. When systems are stressed, by climate events, economic instability, social fragmentation, or political polarization, centralized control cannot respond fast enough, wisely enough, or humanely enough.

This does not mean everyone doing everything, or decision-making by chaos. It means cultivating cultures where responsibility is distributed, trusted, and coordinated. Where people are invited to participate rather than managed into compliance.
Systems become resilient when many people are capable of seeing, responding, and acting within their sphere of influence. When responsibility is shared, adaptability increases. Trust deepens.

For the past century, we have lived inside a familiar pendulum swing: when something no longer works, we rush toward its opposite, hoping correction will come through reversal. But reacting in opposition rarely creates transformation.

It will require trust in people’s capacity to engage thoughtfully. It will require listening across difference, coordinating across sectors, and supporting those willing to do the difficult work of building viable alternatives that the public can understand, trust, and step into.
Not that we wait to be invited or appointed, but that we notice where we are already positioned to contribute. That we move from critique to participation.
